title: AI-led selloff pushes Nasdaq into correction; S&P 500 suffers worst day in about 18 months
content:
US equities fell sharply on 5 November as AI and semiconductor stocks were heavily sold. Sources put the Nasdaq Composite down about **5.5%**, leaving it roughly 10–12% below its October record and in correction territory, while the S&P 500 fell about **4.4%** and the Dow lost more than 1,800 points (around 3.4%). Reports cite doubts over returns on AI capex, expected scrutiny of data-centre permitting and power costs after the Democratic midterm gains, and forced deleveraging by leveraged funds. Exact closing levels differ slightly by source.

Stocks steadied on 6 November, with the Nasdaq up about **1.1%** and the S&P 500 up 0.3%, but the week still ended sharply lower. The move matters beyond one session because mega-cap tech concentration drives index returns and AI funding sentiment, and a strong US payrolls print has kept Fed hike speculation alive.

title: Brent posts steepest weekly fall since 2020 on US-Iran deal hopes; Hormuz still disrupted
content:
Oil fell sharply over the week to 6 November as markets priced a possible US-Iran agreement following the US midterm elections. Brent settled at **$98.32/bbl** on Friday, down from around $106 on 2 November, in its steepest weekly decline since 2020, while WTI settled near **$90.83/bbl**. Qatar is reportedly mediating a draft deal, although Iran reported further tanker attacks in the Strait of Hormuz on Thursday and the waterway remains effectively shut to normal commercial traffic.

Lower crude helped bonds and equities early in the week and eased near-term inflation concerns, but the move rests on diplomacy rather than supply. Goldman Sachs raised its December Brent forecast to $105/bbl, warning of upside risk if Gulf output stays depressed, so energy remains a key driver of the inflation and central bank outlook.

title: BoE raises Bank Rate by 25bp to 4% in 8–1 vote, its first hike since August 2023
content:
The BoE's MPC voted 8–1 on 5 November to raise Bank Rate by 25bp to **4%**, ending a hold at 3.75%. Catherine Mann dissented in favour of a larger **50bp** increase, while Swati Dhingra and Alan Taylor, who had previously backed holding, supported the rise. It is the first increase since August 2023, with higher energy prices cited as a key concern for inflation persistence. The next decision is due on 17 December.

The hike underlines a hawkish turn among major central banks: the Fed held at 3.75–4.00% in October with two dissents for a hike, and the BoJ signalled further tightening. Sources reviewed did not give a clear GBP or gilt reaction. A resilient US labour market and volatile oil leave the December meetings finely balanced.
